comments.text:
Dr. Mike - you should cover the Isle of Man TT races. Serious injuries—such as compound fractures, concussions, and trauma—happen during almost every Isle of Man TT racing and qualifying week. For example, a single race day in 2026 resulted in multiple riders hospitalized, including serious injuries to local racer Jamie Cringle. 
The sidecar race is INSANE. The passenger is hanging off the back of the car - nothing behind them to stop them falling off, as they move from handhold to handhold when shifting their whole body weight. It involves purpose-built three-wheeled outfits piloted by a driver and a passenger on the 37.73-mile Snaefell Mountain Course. Reaching speeds over 160 mph, the sport requires the passenger to actively shift their weight to maintain traction and balance. Following safety incidents, organizers suspended sidecar classes for a sustainability review.

comments.text:
I always say the exact point you made, I’m a paddle boarder and wild swimmer, and being aware that ‘you didn’t evolve for this environment’ is something I wish a lot of other people considered, you’re not designed for water, the ocean, or the air.
Currents will get you, pressure will get you, wind changes will get you, storms will get you - you’re not a bird, or a fish, and you’re not a seal, you aren’t designed to be in this zone, you’re a non-buoyant, non-flying ape, and that’s what keeps me conscious of safety!
Even in something as chill as paddle boarding, tide changes, currents, drowning machines and more can easily kill you or severely injure you (heck it’s been a huge PSA in the SUP community about not wearing your ankle leash in rivers because of drowning machines and severe unseen currents, as when you’re attached to your board which will get dragged down, you can’t unhook yourself and essentially stay tied to a submerged board, there’s been several deaths in the past few years from this minor addition alone) it’s really important to be aware of this stuff!
